text.title: Activation Metrics Core Rules
text.summary: 8 testable rules every Activation Metrics application MUST enforce. HARD rules — user-supplied input cannot override them.

rule.statement: `activation_rate` MUST be computed as users who performed the activation event inside the window divided by ALL users who signed up in the cohort period. The denominator MUST NOT be narrowed to users who reached a later funnel step, users who returned, or "qualified" signups.

rationale.source: Alistair Croll and Benjamin Yoskovitz, Lean Analytics (2013); widely established growth-analytics practice

rule.rationale: Every narrowing of the denominator inflates the rate. A report that quotes 31 percent against "users who opened the app twice" and 12 percent against signups describes the same product; only the second number tells the team what onboarding actually does to a new signup.

rule.statement: The report MUST state one activation window in days (e.g. 7d) and use it for every metric. `period_start` and `period_end` are signup dates. A signup cohort whose `signup_date + window` is later than the data cutoff MUST be excluded from every rate, or reported as a separate metric whose name ends in `_partial`.

rationale.source: widely established cohort-reporting practice; Amplitude retention documentation

rule.rationale: Including the most recent, still-open cohort produces the artificial drop at the right edge that gets reported as a regression week after week. Mixing a 7-day and a 14-day window inside one report makes week-over-week deltas meaningless.

rule.statement: `activation_rate` MUST be reported per acquisition channel (first-touch `utm_source`/`utm_medium` or the channel grouping the team already uses) as separate `metrics[]` entries named `activation_rate__<channel>`, in addition to the aggregate. A segment below the sample floor the report declares MUST be labelled `low_sample` in its finding rather than compared.

rationale.source: Lean Analytics (Croll and Yoskovitz); widely established marketing-analytics practice

rule.rationale: Aggregate activation moves with the channel mix, not with the product: a paid campaign that brings low-intent signups drops the blended rate while onboarding is unchanged. Per-channel rates separate the two, and the sample floor stops a 9-signup channel from headlining the findings.

rule.statement: Time-to-activation MUST be reported as median and at least one upper quantile (p75 or p90) in `unit: hours` or `unit: days`, computed only over activated users. The arithmetic mean MUST NOT be the only time-to-activation figure.

rationale.source: widely established statistics practice for right-skewed duration data

rule.rationale: Activation times are heavily right-skewed; a handful of users activating on day 29 drags the mean far past where most users actually activate, so a "mean 6.4 days" hides that half the users activated within an hour.

rule.statement: For every candidate activation event the report MUST give D30 retention for users who performed it inside the window and for users who did not, together with both group sizes, from a cohort at least 30 days old at the cutoff. The finding MUST describe the difference as correlation, not as the effect of the event.

rationale.source: Amplitude, 'Mastering Retention' playbook; Sean Ellis and Morgan Brown, Hacking Growth (2017)

rule.rationale: A lift quoted without group sizes cannot be distinguished from noise, and a cohort younger than 30 days has no D30 at all, only a projection. The causal wording is the trap: users who invite a teammate retain better because they are already committed, not because the invite made them so.

rule.statement: Each funnel step MUST report users entering, users completing, absolute drop (entering minus completing) and relative drop (absolute drop divided by entering). Steps MUST be ordered as users traverse them, and each step MUST correspond to a tracked event; a step without an event MUST NOT carry numbers.

rationale.source: Lean Analytics (Croll and Yoskovitz); Mixpanel and Amplitude funnel documentation

rule.rationale: Relative drop alone ranks a step reached by 40 users above a step reached by 2,000; absolute drop alone hides a step that loses 90 percent of a small but valuable segment. Both columns are needed to pick the step worth fixing, and numbers for un-tracked steps are estimates masquerading as measurements.

rule.statement: Every `metrics[]` entry MUST use a snake_case `name` and a `unit` from the set `ratio`, `count`, `days`, `hours`, `pp`. Rates MUST be expressed as ratios between 0 and 1, never as percentages; week-over-week changes MUST be in `pp` (percentage points) and computed against the previous period with the same window and cohort definition.
rule.rationale: A value of 31 with no unit is read as 31 percent by one consumer and as 31 users by another, and a "4 percent increase" is ambiguous between 27 to 31 percent and 27 to 28.1 percent. Fixed units make the report machine-readable and the delta unambiguous.

rule.statement: Every string in `findings[]` MUST reference at least one `metrics[].name` from the same report and the comparison period it is measured against. A finding that attributes a change to a product change MUST name that change and its release date, and MUST NOT claim causation unless the change was an A/B test with a stated result.

rationale.source: widely established experimentation practice; Ron Kohavi, Diane Tang and Ya Xu, Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments (2020)

rule.rationale: "Activation improved thanks to the new checklist" is the sentence that gets quoted in the board deck. If the checklist shipped the same week a paid campaign paused, the finding is a channel-mix artefact. Tying each finding to a metric and a period keeps the report auditable.
